content: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is an uncommon but severe pathogen in neonates. Before the introduction of antiviral medications, the mortality rate for neonatal HSV infections was alarmingly high. Specifically, 85% of infants with disseminated HSV infection and 50% of those with HSV encephalitis died within their first year of life. Among survivors of widespread (multiorgan) infection, up to 50% experienced long-term neurological complications. The primary goal of this review was to assess the impact of antiviral agents on mortality, disease progression, and neurodevelopmental outcomes at approximately one year of age in neonates with HSV infection. A secondary objective was to evaluate the potential adverse effects of these antiviral agents, particularly nephrotoxicity and bone marrow suppression. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering publications up to November 2008. Additionally, reference lists of published trials were reviewed. The inclusion criteria were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving infants under one month of age with virologically confirmed HSV infection. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the criteria established by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Statistical analyses, including meta-analyses when feasible, were conducted using RevMan 5.1 to calculate relative risks, risk differences, and their 95% confidence intervals. Two randomized controlled trials involving a total of 273 infants met the inclusion criteria. The first study (Whitley 1980) compared vidarabine to placebo in 63 infants with various forms of neonatal HSV disease, including disseminated disease, central nervous system (CNS) disease, and skin, eye, and mouth (SEM) disease. The second study (Whitley 1991) compared aciclovir to vidarabine in 210 infants. In the Whitley 1980 study, there was no significant reduction in overall mortality when all forms of neonatal HSV disease were analyzed together. However, when data from infants with CNS disease or disseminated disease were combined, a significant reduction in mortality was observed. Despite this, there was no difference in the rate of neurological abnormalities among survivors at one year, whether analyzed as a whole group or by specific disease category. In the Whitley 1991 study, no significant differences were found between aciclovir and vidarabine in terms of reducing mortality, preventing disease progression, or decreasing the incidence of neurological abnormalities at one year. Additionally, there was no significant difference in the rates of drug-induced renal toxicity or bone marrow suppression between the two treatments. For infants with SEM disease, neurological outcomes were similar between those treated with aciclovir and those treated with vidarabine. Both drugs were well tolerated during the neonatal period. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence from clinical trials to definitively evaluate the effects of antiviral agents, either compared to placebo or to each other, in the treatment of neonatal HSV infections. The rarity of neonatal HSV makes it challenging to conduct adequately powered clinical trials. Further research is needed to assess the efficacy of newer antiviral agents with improved bioavailability, such as valaciclovir and valganciclovir, in randomized trials. Additionally, the potential role of oral antiviral formulations should be explored, particularly for treating infants with SEM disease or recurrent HSV infections after the neonatal period.
